title: Little children (1 John 2:12–17)
hookLine: the elder writes tenderly to children, young people and elders

lines: A PET NAME FOR HIS READERS.
cards: Families have pet names. Kiddo. Sweetheart.
Buddy. Some grandparents call grown adults by a childhood nickname to the end, and nobody minds, because it isn't about age. It's about belonging.
The writer of First John has a pet name for his readers, and he keeps coming back to it: little children.
Today he stops the flow of the letter for a little poem, short lines to everyone in the room, young and old, and then a warning about what can pull them away.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "I write unto you, little children, because your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake. I write unto you, fathers, because ye have known him that is from the beginning. I write unto you, young men, because ye have overcome the wicked one."
Then he goes round the circle again. Little children: you're forgiven. Fathers, the older ones: you have known him a long time.
Young people: you are strong, the word of God lives in you, and you've already won a battle. Scholars aren't sure whether he means actual ages, stages of faith, or all three said to everyone at once.
On that last reading, every reader is a little child who is forgiven, a mature one who knows, and a young one who is strong. Notice what he doesn't do: scold.
Every line turns on because: because you're forgiven, because you know, because you've overcome. He writes from what's already true of them.
Then the warning: "Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world." That can sound strange next to John's Gospel, where God so loved the world.
But world here seems to mean something else: the way of life that leaves God out. He names it: "the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life."
Wanting, looking, showing off. Appetite, envy, status.

teach.h: THE WORLD PASSES. THE DOER ABIDES.
teach.b: Then perspective: "And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever."

teach.h: I WRITE UNTO YOU, LITTLE CHILDREN.
teach.b: Trends pass. The one who does the will of God abides.

how: Some churches read 1 John 2:12–14 as a blessing for every age in a congregation, and the warning about the lust of the eyes and the pride of life comes up in teaching on simple living.

o: a tender name the writer uses for all his readers
young pupils in a church school class
the newest believers, not yet old enough to teach

games.q: you're the writer of this letter, and your church is young and old together. how do you open?
o: with a list of their faults.
with what's already true of each of them.
games.why: "I write unto you, little children, because your sins are forgiven you." each group is written to because of what's already true.

practice: Bring to mind someone younger than you, someone older, and a friend your own age.

For each, quietly finish the sentence I'm writing to you because, with something already true of them rather than something they should do: because you're forgiven, because you've taught me, because you're strong.
If you pray, pray for each by name.

wordCard.voice: Little children. The writer's pet name for his readers: forgiven, belonging, written to because of what's already true.

orig.note: Greek: little children, a tender diminutive. used again and again in 1 John.

carryVoice: Your line: the world passeth away. His pet name says you belong. See you tomorrow.
